dispute have already lived with the conflict longer than they wanted to. Our goal is to move the matter toward resolution as efficiently as the process allows.

Use the online form to share your contact information, your organization or firm, and the general type of matter, for instance employment, contract, or personal injury. If the matter is time-sensitive, such as an approaching statute of limitations or court-ordered deadline, please note

that as well. Do not include party or counsel names, dispute facts, pleadings, medical records, settlement communications, or other documents. We respond quickly to every inquiry, and if the matter moves forward, we will explain how to provide the names needed for a conflict check.

17 Birdsong ParkwayOrchard Park, New York 14127716.932.8566smooney@attymooney.com

We create a structured setting for the employees at the center of a workplace conflict to address the issues directly. We do not decide who is right, impose discipline, investigate a claim, or represent a participant.

For leaders, human resources professionals, and counsel, successful mediation offers a resolved conflict, restored working relationships, and a clear record of what was agreed and what remains for the organization to address. We help the people involved understand the issues, hear how the

conflict is affecting the workplace, test possible ways forward, and decide what can change.

Mediation may be worth considering when

A working relationship matters, but direct conversations have stalled.

The conflict is affecting communication, trust, performance, or the broader team.

The people involved need a more disciplined setting than an ordinary meeting provides.

Leadership wants to explore resolution without asking the mediator to make a factual finding.

Another process may need to come first when

Immediate safety, retaliation, or legal-compliance concerns require action.

An organization must investigate facts or make an employment decision.

A participant cannot take part voluntarily or does not understand the process.

A brief conversation with us can clarify the right sequence without requiring detailed facts by email.

Our role

We structure the process, support a productive conversation, and remain neutral. We do not represent a participant or give legal advice.

The participants

Bring their own experience, listen, test options, and decide whether any proposed next step is workable.

The organization, HR, and counsel

Help define authority, logistics, and the relationship between mediation and any separate internal or legal process.

Confidentiality

Confidentiality depends on the setting, applicable law, and the mediation agreement. The boundaries are explained before substantive discussion begins; they should not be assumed from this website.

Before. The organization and participants clarify the purpose, roles, authority, logistics, and confidentiality terms.

During. We set the structure, identify the issues that need attention, and help the participants explore practical options.

After. The participants clarify agreed actions, open questions, ownership, and what will be documented.

Whatever your role in the conflict, you will be treated with respect, professionalism, and understanding throughout the process. We give you a real opportunity to be heard, not just to speak. Mediation gives you a structured way to address what has been difficult to resolve on your own,

work toward a resolution you help shape, and move forward, whether that means a specific agreement, a changed way of working together, or simply a clearer understanding between the people involved.

Download a one-page guide to workplace mediation (PDF)

A structured, confidential conversation guided by a neutral mediator, in which the people involved in a workplace conflict work toward a resolution they shape themselves. The mediator does not decide who is right, impose discipline, or investigate a claim.

Yes. Mediation works because the participants choose to take part. An organization may encourage or arrange mediation, but a participant who cannot take part voluntarily, or who does not understand the process, is not a candidate for it.

The employees at the center of the conflict. Depending on the matter, a leader, human resources professional, or counsel may take part in defining the scope and logistics, but the mediation session itself centers on the people directly involved.

Most workplace mediations are booked for a half-day or full-day session, depending on complexity. Some matters benefit from brief individual conversations before the joint session.

Confidentiality depends on the setting, applicable law, and the mediation agreement. The boundaries are explained to every participant before substantive discussion begins, and they should not be assumed from this website.

No. The mediator remains neutral, does not represent any participant, and does not give legal advice. The outcome belongs to the participants.

Not every mediation ends in a formal agreement, and that is not a failure. Participants often leave with a clearer understanding of the issues, of each other, and of what remains for the organization to address.

No. Where immediate safety, retaliation, or legal-compliance concerns require action, or where the organization must investigate facts or make an employment decision, another process may need to come first. A brief conversation with us can clarify the right sequence.

Send a general inquiry with your contact information and the general nature of the matter. Do not include names or dispute details at that stage. We respond quickly and explain the next step.

Look for real organizational experience. Workplace conflict lives inside reporting lines, budgets, and daily routines. A mediator who has led teams and handled personnel issues from the inside will recognize what is actually driving the conflict.

Confirm independence. The mediator should have no stake in the outcome and no ongoing role with the organization that could compromise neutrality.

Ask how boundaries are explained. A good mediator tells every participant, before the session, what the mediator does and does not do, and how confidentiality will work in that setting.

Ask how power imbalances are handled. Workplace conflict often involves a manager and a direct report. Ask how the mediator makes sure each participant has a real opportunity to be heard.

Understand the legal context without expecting legal advice. A mediator with a legal background can help participants see where a workplace conflict may intersect with legal obligations, while remaining neutral and giving no legal advice to anyone.

Ask what happens afterward. Resolution should not end when the session does. Ask how agreements, open questions, and responsibility for next steps are documented.

Expect responsiveness. People have usually lived with the conflict longer than they wanted to before mediation is considered. A mediator who responds promptly respects that.

Most people involved in a workplace conflict have lived with it longer than they wanted to. By the time mediation is considered, communication has often stalled, trust has eroded, and the conflict is affecting more than the two people at its center. Our approach starts from that reality.

We believe the people in the conflict are the ones best positioned to resolve it, when given a structured setting, a neutral guide, and a real opportunity to be heard. We do not decide who is right. We help participants understand the issues, hear how the conflict is affecting the

workplace, test possible ways forward, and decide what can change.

We bring decades in litigation, executive leadership, and coaching to that work. Litigation experience grounds the discussion in realism. Executive experience brings a working understanding of how organizations actually function. Coaching, including active listening, gives participants

tools to communicate clearly and manage a difficult conversation.

Throughout, every participant is treated with respect, professionalism, and understanding, whatever the outcome. Resolution comes first. Fairness and efficiency are how we get there.

Agreeing to mediate. The organization arranges the mediation and confirms that each participant is taking part voluntarily. Before anything substantive is discussed, we explain the process, the mediator's role, and the confidentiality terms that apply.

A brief individual conversation. Where useful, we speak briefly with each participant before the joint session to understand their perspective and answer questions about the process. This is not a time to argue the conflict, only to prepare for it.

Preparing. Participants do not need to prepare documents or a formal position. It helps to think about what the conflict has been like, what you would need to see change, and what a workable way forward might look like.

The session. Most sessions run a half-day or a full day. We set the structure, identify the issues that need attention, and help participants explore practical options. Joint discussion may be combined with separate conversations with each participant as needed.

Reaching an outcome. Participants decide what they can agree on. That may be a specific agreement, a changed way of working together, or a clearer understanding between the people involved. Not every mediation ends in a formal agreement, and participants are never pressured into one.

Afterward. We help participants clarify agreed actions, open questions, ownership, and what will be documented, so the resolution has a real chance to hold once everyone returns to work.

My path from litigation into executive leadership and coaching shapes how I help parties reach resolution. Nearly two decades trying and arguing cases at the trial and appellate level, in both state and federal court, gave me a realistic sense of how a case actually resolves, so I can help

parties weigh their options with that same realism rather than in the abstract. The years since, leading teams and responding directly to personnel issues, gave me a practical understanding of how organizations make decisions and where conflict tends to get stuck, informing a process built

for efficiency as well as resolution. My training as a Certified Leadership Coach, including active listening, gives participants the tools to communicate clearly, manage difficult conversations, and identify what they actually need, in service of a fair outcome for everyone at the table.

Across all of this, I bring empathy and a working understanding of what daily life inside an organization is actually like, for a party to a legal claim, an employee, or a manager alike.

As a mediator, I do not represent either side or decide the outcome. I organize the process, explain its boundaries, and guide participants toward a resolution they help shape themselves.

This Privacy Policy explains how The Mooney Firm (“the firm,” “we,” “us,” or “our”) handles information in connection with this website, www.attymooney.com (the “website”). This website provides information and a limited general inquiry form. It is not a secure intake, document,

scheduling, or payment system. Please read this notice before submitting information through the website.

1. Information we collect

General inquiry form

The form collects your name, email address, and general inquiry type. If you choose to provide them, it also collects your telephone number, organization or firm, a time-sensitive flag with an optional brief timing note, and a brief administrative note. The form does not ask for party or

Technical records

The hosting provider may process technical records needed to deliver and protect the site, such as an internet protocol address, browser information, request time, and requested page. The site does not intentionally use advertising or cross-site tracking cookies.

The website uses Resend, configured through Strelva’s mail infrastructure, to deliver the form fields to The Mooney Firm by email. The site does not add the submission to a separate website database. Hosting, delivery, and recipient email providers may process records needed to operate and

protect their services.

3. How we use information

Information collected through the website is used only to:

Respond to your inquiry

Determine whether the firm can assist you

Maintain the security and proper operation of the website

Submitting the form or contacting the firm through the website does not create an attorney-client relationship. An attorney-client relationship is formed only through a written agreement signed by both you and the firm.

4. No secure intake through the website

Do not use the form or an initial email to send confidential communications, dispute details, mediation submissions, or documents. If more information is needed, the firm can identify an appropriate channel.

The website does not intentionally use advertising or cross-site tracking cookies, and it does not currently use analytics services. If this changes, this notice will be updated to describe the tools used and the choices available to you.

With service providers who host, deliver, or protect the website and its email infrastructure, subject to their own operational and security practices

When required by law or legal process

To protect the rights, property, or safety of the firm or others

7. Direct email, telephone, and external links

Direct email, telephone calls, and any external links on the website are subject to the privacy and security practices of those channels or destination services, not this notice. Please limit an initial contact to the information requested on the contact page unless the firm has confirmed

another delivery method.

8. Data retention

The firm retains information collected through the website only as long as necessary to respond to your inquiry, determine whether the firm can assist you, and comply with applicable professional and legal obligations.

9. Data security

The firm and its service providers take reasonable measures to protect information submitted through the website. No website or electronic transmission is completely secure, and the firm cannot guarantee absolute security. This is a further reason not to submit confidential or sensitive

information through the website.

10. Children’s privacy

This website is not directed to individuals under the age of thirteen, and the firm does not knowingly collect personal information from children through the website.

11. Notice to California residents

This section applies to visitors who reside in California and supplements the other sections of this notice. It is provided under the California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (together, the “CCPA”).

Categories of personal information collected

In the preceding twelve months, the website has collected the following categories of personal information, as defined under the CCPA: identifiers, such as your name, email address, and telephone number; and other information you voluntarily provide, such as your organization or firm and

the content of your inquiry. The website does not collect sensitive personal information, and it does not collect the categories described in the other sections of this notice, such as biometric information, geolocation, or internet browsing history beyond the basic technical records

described above.

Sources and purposes

The firm collects this information directly from you when you submit the general inquiry form. The firm uses this information only for the purposes described in Section 3 above, which are to respond to your inquiry, determine whether the firm can assist you, and maintain the security and

proper operation of the website.

No sale or sharing of personal information

To exercise any of these rights, contact the firm using the information in Section 13 below. The firm will take reasonable steps to verify your identity before responding to a request. You may also designate an authorized agent to submit a request on your behalf, subject to verification of

Not all inquiries are responded to or accepted as engagements. The firm cannot serve as your legal representative or as a mediator in any matter unless you and the firm expressly agree in writing to the scope of the engagement. You should assume that the firm does not represent you and is

taking no action on your behalf to protect your rights or interests unless you have signed a written agreement with the firm and, thereafter, received written confirmation from the firm that it is handling your matter.

5. No warranty; no guarantee of outcome
